marimo: notebooks that stay in sync, in any browser

The problem it solves

Classic notebooks lie. Cells can be run in any order, so a stale cell happily shows numbers from a variable you have since changed. The file is a blob of JSON that makes a mess of git diffs, it cannot be imported or run as a script, and SQL, the language I would rather use for most data questions, sits awkwardly in a Python cell. And a notebook server that I can reach from a second computer usually takes an afternoon to set up.

The general idea

marimo is a reactive notebook. Cells form a dependency graph: change a value and every cell that reads it re-runs automatically, so what you see is always consistent with the code. A notebook is a plain Python file, which is friendly to git, can be run as a script and imported as a module. SQL cells are built in and are executed with DuckDB, and UI elements such as sliders and dropdowns turn an analysis into a small app. For exploring data, it is the most productive tool I have found.

Examples

import marimo as mo

rooms = mo.ui.slider(1, 10, value=3)   # one cell

df = mo.sql(f"""                         # another cell, in SQL
    SELECT city, count(*) AS n
    FROM prices
    WHERE rooms >= {rooms.value}
    GROUP BY city
""")

Move the slider and the SQL cell, and everything below it, updates. From the command line:

marimo edit analysis.py     # open or create a notebook in the browser
marimo run analysis.py      # serve it as a read-only app

Tips from my setup

  • Open it remotely. A just marimo recipe starts the server on the computer at home that is always on: uv run marimo edit . --host 0.0.0.0 --port 6061 --watch --no-token. Over Tailscale I open it from the laptop, the iPad or the phone, and the heavy queries run at home. That token-free setup is only sensible because the machine is on my private network, nothing is exposed to the internet. See the post about data science from anywhere.
  • Edit in Neovim, see it in the browser. The --watch flag reloads the notebook when the file changes on disk, so I can edit the Python file in my editor while the browser shows the result.
  • SQL cells on my DuckDB files. A SQL cell queries the project database directly, and the next Python cell continues with the result as a dataframe. See the post about DuckDB.
  • Settings: vim keybindings, autosave after one second, a compact layout and basedpyright for type checking.
  • Notebooks are code. They live in a notebooks/ folder of the project as plain Python files, with marimo as one of the project's dependencies, so uv run marimo works on any machine.
